clinicalPearls: AGel is an autosomal dominant amyloidosis caused by mutations in the gelsolin gene (GSN), classically Asp187Asn, first described in Finland.
The characteristic clinical triad is corneal lattice dystrophy, cranial neuropathy (especially facial) and cutis laxa.
Corneal lattice dystrophy is usually the earliest feature, appearing in early adulthood, and may cause visual disturbance and recurrent erosions.
A slowly progressive facial neuropathy produces a mask-like drooping face, bulbar symptoms and, later, a peripheral polyneuropathy.
The skin becomes lax and prematurely aged, and blepharochalasis can impair vision.
Renal and cardiac involvement are usually mild and life expectancy is often near-normal, which distinguishes AGel from most systemic amyloidoses.
Diagnosis is clinical in affected kindreds and confirmed by GSN sequencing; management is supportive, including ophthalmic and reconstructive surgery.
reference.pathophysiology: Gelsolin is an actin-binding protein important in cytoskeletal remodelling. Amyloidogenic GSN mutations disrupt calcium binding and expose an abnormal cleavage site, so that aberrant proteolysis generates a fragment that misfolds and forms amyloid fibrils. These deposit preferentially along cranial and peripheral nerves, in the cornea and basement membranes, and in dermal connective tissue, producing the characteristic neuro-ophthalmic and cutaneous phenotype. Visceral deposition is comparatively limited, which explains the relatively benign systemic course, although the disease is nonetheless slowly progressive over decades.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of corneal lattice dystrophy
Other cranial neuropathies including sarcoidosis and idiopathic facial palsy
Other hereditary and acquired peripheral neuropathies
Sjögren syndrome for the dry eyes
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmological slit-lamp examination for corneal lattice dystrophy
Nerve conduction studies and clinical neurological assessment
Skin or other tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and typing if the diagnosis is unclear
Assessment of renal and cardiac function to gauge systemic involvement
redFlags: Progressive facial weakness accompanying corneal disease
Bulbar symptoms causing swallowing or speech difficulty
New significant proteinuria or cardiac symptoms suggesting atypical systemic burden
reference.prognosis: The course is slowly progressive over decades with predominantly neuro-ophthalmic and cutaneous morbidity. Life expectancy is usually near-normal, although quality of life is affected by facial palsy, ocular disease and skin laxity.
pitfalls: Dismissing corneal lattice dystrophy as isolated when it heralds a systemic hereditary disease
Misdiagnosing the facial neuropathy as idiopathic facial palsy
Assuming that all amyloidoses share a poor prognosis and over-treating
references: Oxford Textbook of Medicine, chapter on hereditary amyloidosis
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology, section on amyloid neuropathy
International Society of Amyloidosis nomenclature guidelines
management: No disease-modifying therapy is established, so management is supportive and organ-directed with a generally favourable systemic outlook
Ocular care for corneal lattice dystrophy with lubricants for recurrent erosions and corneal grafting for visual failure, though deposits may recur
Protection of the exposed eye in progressive facial neuropathy, and oculoplastic surgery for blepharochalasis and lid laxity impairing vision
Symptomatic treatment of the slowly progressive facial and peripheral polyneuropathy, with speech and swallowing support for bulbar involvement
Periodic assessment of renal and cardiac function to detect the usually mild systemic deposition
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant GSN disease and screening of at-risk relatives
Coordinate ophthalmology, neurology and dermatology input through a specialist amyloidosis service
